title: Ecclesiastes 3:1–8
context: Ecclesiastes 3:1–8 is the poem of times, kept here as one unit. After the opening line, “For everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven”, fourteen pairs of opposites move from birth and death through planting, healing, mourning, embracing, speaking, love, and war. The book presents these words as those of “the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem” (1:1). Jewish and Christian tradition has long associated the Preacher with Solomon, while many interpreters read the royal voice as a literary persona and date the book later; this draft takes no position on authorship or date. Ecclesiastes is wisdom literature, and much of it speaks from the perspective of life “under the sun”, observing the world as it appears to human experience. The poem describes the rhythms of life without saying whether each time is to be chosen, endured, or both, and readers differ on how much it describes God’s ordering and how much it describes the seasons people must recognize. Some lines, such as casting away and gathering stones, are of uncertain meaning. Both traditions read the poem as shared ground: human life unfolds in seasons that people do not control, and wisdom lies in discerning the time.

verses.text: For everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven:
verses.arminianNotes:
The poem opens, “For everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven”. The line governs the whole poem that follows.

Arminian readers note that the seasons of life call for wise and responsible discernment, and they see human beings invited to recognize the fitting time for action within the world God has made.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the opening line speaks of appointed times, and they see in it a confession that the course of life lies within God’s ordering rather than human control, a theme the Preacher develops in 3:11 and 3:14.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and do not use it to reopen the questions treated at Proverbs 16:9.

verses.text: a time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted;
verses.arminianNotes:
The first pair sets birth against death, and the second sets planting against plucking up what is planted. The poem begins with the boundaries of every life and the rhythm of the agricultural year.

Arminian readers note that some of these times are chosen, such as planting, while others, such as birth and death, are received, and they see wisdom as acting rightly within both kinds of time.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see birth and death placed beyond human choosing, so that the poem from the start reminds readers that life is given and taken within God’s purposes, while planting and harvest belong to the ordered world he sustains.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the givenness and the rhythm of human life.

verses.text: a time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up;
verses.arminianNotes:
The poem sets a time to kill against a time to heal, and a time to break down against a time to build up. The pairs are stark.

Arminian readers note that the poem describes what happens in human life without approving every act it names, and they caution against reading the line as license for violence, since the book elsewhere laments oppression (4:1).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read the poem descriptively, and they note that Scripture recognizes contexts such as judgment or war in which taking life occurs, while also valuing healing and building. The precise situations the poet has in mind are not stated.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and avoid drawing a general ethic of killing from a poem about seasons.

verses.text: a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
verses.arminianNotes:
There is a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance. The emotional life of people has its seasons as well.

Arminian readers see permission for honest grief and genuine joy, and they note that faithful people need not pretend to feel what the moment does not call for, since God made room for both sorrow and celebration in human life.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the pairing of mourning and dancing recalls the reversals of the psalms (compare Psalm 30:11), and they see the seasons of sorrow and joy as held within God’s care, even when their reasons are hidden.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and as pastoral encouragement to receive each season honestly before God.

verses.text: a time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;
verses.arminianNotes:
There is a time to cast away stones and a time to gather stones together, a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embracing. The meaning of the line about stones is uncertain; suggestions include clearing or preparing a field, building, and other customs, and none is certain.

Arminian readers note that wisdom includes knowing when closeness is fitting and when restraint is right.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hold the meaning of the stones lightly and read the line as part of the poem’s picture of opposite actions, each fitting at its own time.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and avoid building interpretation on an uncertain image, preferring the poem’s general point about the timing of human actions.

verses.text: a time to seek, and a time to lose; a time to keep, and a time to cast away;
verses.arminianNotes:
There is a time to seek and a time to lose, a time to keep and a time to cast away. Possessions, too, have their seasons.

Arminian readers note that the line calls for wisdom about when to pursue something and when to let it go, and they see in this a freedom from clinging to things that cannot last, which fits the book’s concern about restless labor (4:8).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the line as teaching contentment, since what is kept or lost is finally held within God’s ordering, and they note that the book repeatedly warns against finding security in what one gathers (2:18; 5:10).

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about holding possessions lightly.

verses.text: a time to tear, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak;
verses.arminianNotes:
There is a time to tear and a time to sew, a time to keep silence and a time to speak. The tearing may recall the tearing of garments in mourning, though the text does not say so.

Arminian readers note that speech and silence are both responsible choices, and they see wisdom as discerning when a word will help and when it is better withheld.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Scripture often commends restraint in speech (compare 5:2), and they see the line as calling for words that fit the moment, a gift of wisdom that comes from God.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about discernment in speech and in the outward expressions of grief and restoration.

verses.text: a time to love, and a time to hate; a time for war, and a time for peace.
verses.arminianNotes:
The poem closes, “a time to love, and a time to hate; a time for war, and a time for peace.” The final pairs move from personal relationships to the life of nations.

Arminian readers note that the poem describes real human experience, and they read the time to hate in light of Scripture’s call to hate evil, not people, while recognizing that the verse itself does not explain the object.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note that the poem does not define what is to be loved or hated, and they read the closing pairs as part of a world under God’s rule, in which war and peace come and go.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and the poem’s ending as preparing for the reflections of 3:9–15.
